title: One-Way and Two-Way Door Decisions
seoTitle: One-Way and Two-Way Door Decisions | Chase Arenella
description: Sort decisions by how easily they can be reversed, then give each one the right amount of process. A short guide to one-way and two-way doors.
answer: A one-way door decision is hard or costly to undo. A two-way door decision can be reversed cheaply. Sorting choices this way tells you how much process each one deserves.

sections.heading: The two doors
paragraphs: A two-way door is a choice you can walk back through. If it goes badly, you reverse it, and the cost is small. A one-way door is a choice that is hard, expensive, or impossible to undo. Once you are through, you live with the result.

Most decisions are two-way doors. Teams often treat them like one-way doors anyway, so they add reviews, meetings, and sign-offs to choices that a quick test would settle. The goal is not to decide faster everywhere. It is to spend process where it buys something.

sections.heading: How to sort a choice
paragraphs: Reversibility is a matter of degree, so ask a few direct questions before you pick a process. Answer them in order and stop when you have a clear read.

items: What does it cost to undo this, in money, time, and trust?
How long until we would know it was wrong?
Who else is affected, and can they absorb a reversal?
Can we shrink it into a smaller, reversible version first?

sections.heading: Matching process to the door
paragraphs: For two-way doors, name one owner, set a short deadline, and decide with the information at hand. Write down what would make you reverse it. Then act. A wrong call you catch in a week costs less than a right call you reach in a month.

For one-way doors, slow down on purpose. Gather outside views, ask someone to argue the opposite case, and record the reasoning in a decision log. AI can help by surfacing options and risks, but the final call stays with a named person. Competitive players make the same split: adjusting positioning mid-round is cheap, while committing every resource to a single round is not.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
paragraphs: The sorting step can go wrong in predictable ways. Watch for these patterns.

items: False one-way doors. Fear makes a reversible choice feel permanent. Ask what reversing it would actually take.
Hidden one-way doors. A small pilot becomes permanent once customers, contracts, or public promises depend on it.
Slow reversals. A door is only two-way if you notice the problem in time. Long feedback delays quietly lock it.
Never closing the door. Reversible does not mean endlessly revisited. Set a review date and hold the decision until then.

faqs.q: What is a one-way door decision?
faqs.a: It is a choice that is costly or impossible to reverse, such as a major hire, a public commitment, or a platform migration. These deserve slower, more careful review.

faqs.q: How do you know if a decision is reversible?
faqs.a: Estimate the cost and time to undo it, and how soon you would see it failing. If both are low, treat it as a two-way door.
